strengths: Originality/significance: The paper identifies a useful problem—text-controlled amodal 3D completion when visible evidence admits multiple interpretations—and the separation between observation preservation and semantic completion is intuitive and practically relevant.

Soundness (empirical merits): RelaxFlow improves both TRELLIS and SAM3D on ExtremeOcc-3D; for example, SAM3D Point-FID decreases from 100.38 to 81.11 and CLIP-text rises from 24.08 to 27.26. Ablations attribute gains to low-pass relaxation, visibility masking, and multiple priors.

Presentation: The main pipeline, shared-state dual-branch sampling, temporal cutoff, and visibility-aware SLAT fusion are explained clearly. Qualitative branching examples effectively illustrate the desired behavior.

Reproducibility/limitations: The paper reports principal hyperparameters, backbone stages, hardware, prior construction, benchmark curation, metric definitions, and a candid failure case for mutually incompatible observation/prior pairs.
weaknesses: Soundness: The headline theoretical claim that attention-logit smoothing is equivalent to low-pass filtering the generative vector field is not established. Appendix A.4 only assumes Lipschitz dependence on logits and bounds the magnitude of the induced velocity perturbation; it does not show that blurring logits performs spatial low-pass convolution of the velocity field.

Soundness: Proposition A.4 has a substantive gap. In general, v_sem-G*v_theta=(v_sem-G*v_sem)+G*(v_sem-v_theta), but the proof drops the first, signal-distortion term. Band limitation does not imply invariance under Gaussian filtering except under stronger assumptions. The appendix also refers to an undefined beta in the proposition.

Soundness: The stability derivation incorrectly pulls the time-varying alpha_t outside integrals as though it were constant. The later Wasserstein result consequently is not justified, and it does not prove RelaxFlow is closer to ground truth because the added prior-mismatch term may exceed any claimed error reduction.

Methodological justification: Concatenating prior-token sequences does not by itself guarantee “consensus”; softmax attention need not amplify shared semantics or cancel instance details. Likewise, Gaussian filtering over sequence indices lacks a clear geometric-frequency interpretation, particularly across concatenated priors and sparse or flattened tokens.

Evaluation/significance: AmbiSem-3D contains only 21 manually designed cases. The manuscript gives no selection protocol, inter-annotator agreement, uncertainty estimates, or evidence against cherry-picking. The 32-person user study omits question wording, randomization, participant characteristics, repeated-measures treatment, and statistical significance.

Evaluation: The evidence does not support “strict” observation preservation. Minimum LPIPS selects the best match among ten predicted views rather than evaluating the known input viewpoint, and CLIP-image similarity averages against ground-truth multiview renders plus the observation. Neither directly verifies pixel- or geometry-level preservation at observed surfaces. Results also lack confidence intervals or multi-seed analysis.

Comparisons are not fully diagnostic: the primary baselines are largely not designed to consume the same text/prior signal, while stronger simple dual-condition fusion controls are missing. The ablation without low-pass relaxation helps, but does not isolate logit smoothing from alternative regularization or fusion choices.

Reproducibility/presentation: Essential details remain unspecified, including solver step count, random seeds, exact attention layers and boundary handling used for smoothing, checkpoint/configuration identifiers, benchmark/code release, and complete prior-generation settings. The claim of “negligible computational overhead” is unsupported by runtime or memory measurements and overlooks the second backbone evaluation per solver step.

Limitations/ethics: The conflict failure mode is honestly discussed, but benchmark scope, generated-prior bias, dataset licensing, and user-study consent/compensation are not addressed. The main text and appendix also contain notation inconsistencies, proof typos, and incorrect table references. Overall, the promising empirical idea does not compensate for invalid central theory and insufficiently rigorous evaluation.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper identifies a useful problem—text-controlled amodal 3D completion when one observation admits multiple plausible objects—and the distinction between preserving visible evidence and steering hidden geometry is practically meaningful.

Method/presentation: RelaxFlow has a clear high-level design: observation and semantic-prior branches, multi-prior conditioning, early-step fusion, and visibility-aware blending. The main figures communicate the intended behavior well, and the failure-case appendix honestly identifies incompatible observation/prior conditions.

Empirical promise: Results are reported with two image-to-3D backbones. On ExtremeOcc-3D, the SAM3D variant improves CLIP-text from 24.08 to 27.26 and Point-FID from 100.38 to 81.11, while the component ablations show degradations without logit smoothing or the visibility mask.

Evaluation breadth: The paper combines image-level, text-alignment, perceptual, multi-view, 3D-feature, qualitative, and user-preference evaluations, and introduces two diagnostic test sets targeting extreme occlusion and semantic branching.
weaknesses: Soundness—the central theoretical claim is unsupported. The manuscript repeatedly claims that attention-logit smoothing is “equivalent” to low-pass filtering the generative vector field, but Appendix A.4 establishes only a Lipschitz bound on the magnitude of the induced velocity change. It does not show that the change is a convolution, is low-pass in latent-state frequency, or filters the frequency components assumed in Proposition A.4. Smoothing query/key token indices—especially concatenated tokens from different prior images—has no demonstrated correspondence to Fourier frequencies of the velocity field.

The error-reduction proposition is effectively assumed rather than proved. Assumptions A.2–A.3 posit that ideal semantics are low-frequency and nearly all error is high-frequency. Moreover, the proof replaces v_sem−G*v_theta with G*(v_sem−v_theta), neglecting the signal-distortion term v_sem−G*v_sem; band limitation does not imply a Gaussian exactly preserves all low-frequency components. The statement also invokes an undefined “beta.” Thus the claimed strict reduction need not hold.

The Wasserstein analysis does not substantiate improved generation quality. It inherits the unsupported error-reduction result, introduces unobservable oracle fields and conditioning distances, hides potentially large factors in constants, and only gives upper bounds. The added delta_prior term means RelaxFlow's bound is not necessarily tighter than the standard flow's. There are also inconsistencies in trajectory conditions, time-varying alpha handling, and norm/error notation.

The empirical comparison is not sufficiently controlled for the central claim. Several baselines cannot consume the text/prior information supplied to RelaxFlow, so their weaker prompt alignment is expected. Treating a semantically different prior as an additional TRELLIS view violates that model's same-instance multi-view assumption. Missing comparisons include stronger generic multi-condition/flow-composition methods and carefully matched alternatives using the same priors, fusion schedule, and compute budget.

The metrics do not convincingly demonstrate strict observation preservation or instance-level 3D correctness. Minimum LPIPS over ten predicted views can select a view different from the observation camera; CLIP-image averages against ground-truth multi-view renders; and FID/Point-FID are dataset-level distributional statistics. These can improve through category matching without preserving the observed pixels or producing the correct per-instance geometry. No direct visible-region reprojection, mask-conditioned reconstruction, or geometric error is reported despite ground-truth meshes in ExtremeOcc-3D.

The evaluation is too small and statistically incomplete. AmbiSem-3D contains only 21 manually designed cases, while no category breakdown, repeated-seed results, confidence intervals, or significance tests are provided for either benchmark. The 32-person study omits task wording, randomization, number of judgments, aggregation procedure, participant recruitment/demographics, compensation, and uncertainty estimates; its large preference percentages therefore cannot be independently interpreted.

Reproducibility is inadequate. There is no code or benchmark-release statement, and important details are missing: checkpoint/version information, sampling step count, exact attention layers/heads modified, tensor ordering and boundary handling for concatenated priors, random seeds and retrieved-prior identities, renderer/camera protocol, and computational cost. The claim of “negligible” overhead is especially doubtful because two network velocities are evaluated per solver step; parallel evaluation does not make the added FLOPs or memory negligible, and no timing or memory measurements are given.

The multi-prior consensus argument is heuristic: concatenating tokens does not guarantee that shared attributes receive consensus attention, because softmax normalization, token counts, viewpoint differences, and duplicated irrelevant attributes can change the result. The prior-count ablation is very limited and does not isolate this claimed mechanism.

Presentation and limitations need substantial revision. The paper is readable at a conceptual level, but contains numerous typographical and mathematical inconsistencies. The limitations section discusses only mutually conflicting conditions and omits dependence on prior-generator quality and bias, pose/mask accuracy, token ordering, benchmark scale, and doubled model evaluation. Research-ethics treatment is absent, including consent/privacy details for the user study and potential biases inherited from retrieval and text-to-image priors. Overall, the promising task formulation does not compensate for unsupported theoretical claims and an evaluation that cannot yet establish the central fidelity and mechanism claims.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful and underexplored problem: resolving genuinely ambiguous amodal 3D completion with explicit textual intent while retaining visible evidence. This task framing is original and potentially significant for controllable asset generation, robotics, and AR/VR.

RelaxFlow is a practical, training-free construction that combines observation and semantic-prior branches, early-step velocity blending, multi-prior conditioning, and visibility-aware fusion. Demonstrating the approach on both SAM3D and TRELLIS supports some backbone generality.

The empirical results are promising. On ExtremeOcc-3D, the SAM3D variant improves CLIP-text from 24.08 to 27.26, FID from 50.73 to 39.44, and Point-FID from 100.38 to 81.11 while slightly improving the reported observation metrics. The qualitative examples also show meaningful prompt-dependent structural changes.

Ablations cover relaxation, visibility masking, prior source and count, and key hyperparameters. The large user-study preference on AmbiSem-3D provides useful supporting evidence beyond automatic CLIP metrics.

The presentation is generally clear and visually effective. Implementation hyperparameters and visibility-mask equations are documented, and the appendix honestly illustrates an important failure mode when observation and prior conflict.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is not established. Proposition A.4 effectively treats v_sem-Gσ*vθ as Gσ*(v_sem-vθ), omitting the bias term (I-Gσ)*v_sem. Approximate low-frequency preservation and the non-quantitative condition that high-frequency error is “dominant” do not imply strict error reduction. The proof also refers to an undefined beta. More fundamentally, Appendix A.4 only bounds the change in velocity under logit perturbation; it does not prove that Gaussian smoothing of attention logits is equivalent to Gaussian low-pass filtering of the generative vector field, as repeatedly claimed.

The stability analysis contains consequential inconsistencies: time-varying α is pulled outside trajectory integrals; conditions switch among c_obs, c_sem, and c_prior within definitions and proofs; several trajectory variables are confused; and the Grönwall factors differ between compared bounds. Even accepting the assumptions, E_sem(tilde v)<E_sem(bar v) does not show RelaxFlow has a tighter final bound because the prior-mismatch term is positive. The theoretical contribution should therefore be substantially corrected or reframed as intuition.

The evidence does not adequately support the strong claim of “strictly preserving” observations. Minimum LPIPS selects the best of ten generated views rather than evaluating the known observation camera and visible mask, while CLIP-image averages against ground-truth multiview renders and is not a pixel- or geometry-level preservation measure. ExtremeOcc-3D provides ground-truth geometry and poses, so visible-region reprojection error and visible-surface 3D error should be reported.

AmbiSem-3D contains only 21 manually designed cases. The user study reports percentages from 32 volunteers but omits assignment design, randomization, instructions, number of judgments, quality control, uncertainty, and statistical testing. The small CLIP-text differences also lack confidence intervals or multi-seed variation. These omissions limit confidence in the generality of the headline controllability result.

The baseline coverage does not isolate whether the contribution comes from the proposed relaxation rather than simply supplying category-matched visual priors. Stronger comparisons should include direct prior/attention injection and alternative multi-condition flow-composition or smoothing strategies under matched compute. The ablation reports mainly Point-FID and does not test observation preservation, prompt following, or statistical variability for each component.

Reproducibility is incomplete: there is no stated code or benchmark release, and important details such as which attention layers are modified, padding and boundary handling for concatenated prior-token sequences, prompt lists, sampling seeds, and evaluation implementation are missing. The claim of negligible overhead is also unsupported; evaluating two branches entails roughly doubled model computation even if parallel execution reduces latency, yet runtime and memory measurements are absent.

The limitations discussion is useful but too narrow. It does not address dependence on the quality and biases of retrieved/generated priors, erroneous or adversarial prompts, failures of pose/visibility estimation, category leakage from oracle-like labels, dataset licensing, or consent and compensation procedures for the human study. These are not necessarily prohibitive ethical concerns, but they should be documented.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper identifies a useful controllability problem—using language to disambiguate unseen 3D structure while retaining observed evidence—and the semantic-branch/observation-branch decomposition is intuitive and potentially useful.

Soundness: RelaxFlow is demonstrated on two substantially different flow-based backbones, SAM3D and TRELLIS, and generally improves the reported metrics over each backbone. Component ablations support contributions from logit smoothing, visibility masking, and multiple priors.

Evaluation breadth: The paper includes 264 highly occluded examples, a small diagnostic semantic-branching set, a 100-case extension, comparisons with several alternative pipelines, a 32-participant preference study, runtime measurements, and many multiview qualitative examples.

Presentation: The method and motivation are communicated clearly, the pipeline figures are effective, and implementation choices such as sigma, cutoff, prior count, and visibility-mask parameters are documented.
Limitations and ethics: The authors disclose runtime overhead and failure under conflicting conditions, and include an impact statement acknowledging misuse and inherited bias risks.
weaknesses: Soundness—the principal theoretical claim is unsupported. Proposition A.4 analyzes Gaussian convolution of the velocity field over its input domain, whereas the implementation blurs cross-attention logits along token indices. Appendix A.4 establishes only a Lipschitz bound on how much the velocity changes after modifying logits; it does not establish that the induced change is a low-pass filter on the velocity field, preserves semantic components, or reduces semantic error. Thus the abstract and contribution list overstate an unproven equivalence.

The proof of Proposition A.4 drops the term v_sem-G_sigma*v_sem when treating the post-filter error as G_sigma*epsilon. A Gaussian does not exactly preserve a merely band-limited signal. The proposition also refers to a sufficiently small undefined beta, while the claimed strict improvement depends almost entirely on strong, unvalidated assumptions that semantic structure is low-frequency and estimator error is high-frequency.

The ODE/Wasserstein derivation contains material inconsistencies: time-varying alpha is pulled outside time integrals; conditioning arguments change between c_obs, c_sem, and c_prior; some state variables are mismatched; and Theorem A.9 drops conditioning-mismatch terms appearing in Theorem A.8. Even its stated bounds do not prove RelaxFlow is closer than the standard flow unless the uncontrolled prior mismatch is smaller than the gain. The statement that W2 ensures geometrically plausible shapes is also unjustified.

The central claim of strict observation preservation is not adequately measured. The reported LPIPS is the minimum between the observed render and any of ten predicted views rather than a comparison rendered at the known observation camera. CLIP_img averages ground-truth multiview and observation embeddings, so it conflates observation adherence with overall similarity. Neither metric verifies visible-region pixel or geometric consistency.

The visibility mechanism appears mismatched to the external-occlusion setting. It constructs a z-buffer from generated object voxels and marks the frontmost object surface visible, but the equations do not incorporate the input visibility mask or external blockers. Consequently, a front-facing surface hidden by another scene object can be treated as observed and protected from semantic guidance.

The claimed multi-prior consensus is heuristic: concatenating tokens does not guarantee that common attributes receive more aggregate softmax attention. Moreover, one-dimensional smoothing over flattened query/key sequences can mix spatially nonadjacent tokens and cross prior-image boundaries; these implementation effects are neither analyzed nor ablated against simpler regularization or branch blending.

Evaluation uncertainty is not reported: there are no repeated seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. AmbiSem-3D has only 21 manually designed cases, while its 100-case extension compares only against SAM3D and yields modest automatic-metric gains. ExtremeOcc-3D supplies same-category reference images to the proposed method, making comparisons against baselines without equivalent access to category information difficult to interpret as method-specific gains.

The user study lacks essential reproducibility and ethics details, including the exact comparison protocol, randomization or blinding, number of judgments, participant recruitment, consent and compensation, and uncertainty analysis. Preference percentages alone cannot establish reliability.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite several supplied hyperparameters: the manuscript gives no code or benchmark release information, random seeds, exact solver and attention-layer modification details, or complete generated-prior prompts. Reliance on an external text-to-image generator and a commercial editing baseline further complicates exact replication.

Presentation is polished, but terminology such as “strictly preserving,” “provably reduces,” and “equivalent to applying a low-pass filter” is substantially stronger than the evidence. The empirical idea remains promising, but the theoretical and evaluation issues affect the paper's central claims rather than peripheral details.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper identifies a useful problem—text-guided resolution of ambiguity in amodal image-to-3D generation—and the distinction between preserving observed evidence and softly controlling unobserved structure is intuitively valuable.

Method: The training-free dual-branch construction is practically appealing, supports two different backbones (SAM3D and TRELLIS), and combines multiple semantic priors, time-dependent blending, and visibility-aware fusion in a coherent pipeline.

Evidence: Reported results improve both backbones on ExtremeOcc-3D, with substantial Point-FID and FID gains. Component ablations indicate that low-pass relaxation and visibility masking both contribute, while the qualitative branching examples demonstrate meaningful prompt-dependent changes.

Presentation/limitations: The paper is generally well organized and visually clear. It reports runtime and memory costs, tests generated versus retrieved priors, includes additional baseline families and a 100-case extension, and honestly illustrates failures under incompatible conditions.
weaknesses: Soundness—invalid theoretical bridge: The headline claim that attention-logit blurring is equivalent to low-pass filtering the generative vector field is not proved. Appendix A.4 only bounds the magnitude of the velocity change under an assumed logit-to-velocity Lipschitz property; it establishes neither convolution nor frequency-selective filtering of the output velocity field.

Soundness—faulty spectral argument: Proposition A.4 effectively treats v_sem−G*v_theta as G*(v_sem−v_theta), which requires the Gaussian filter to preserve v_sem exactly. The paper assumes only approximate preservation. Gaussian filtering can attenuate low-frequency semantic signal as well as error, so strict error reduction does not follow from the stated qualitative spectral-dominance assumption. The undefined reference to a “sufficiently small beta” further undermines the proposition.

Soundness—ODE/Wasserstein derivation errors and overclaiming: The stability proof pulls time-varying factors alpha_t outside integrals where alpha_tau should remain inside, contains inconsistent conditions and trajectories, and compresses different Grönwall factors into a common constant. Even its final bound does not show RelaxFlow is closer than the standard flow because RelaxFlow adds the uncontrolled delta_prior term and may have a different constant. Thus the claimed generation-quality guarantee is unsupported.

Evaluation does not establish the central observation-fidelity claim. On ExtremeOcc-3D, CLIP_img averages similarity to ground-truth multiview renders plus the observation, while min-LPIPS selects the best among ten predicted views rather than comparing a camera-aligned render to the visible pixels. Neither metric verifies “strict” preservation of observed regions. Given available meshes, masks, poses, and depths, visible-region silhouette, RGB, depth, or geometry errors should have been reported.

The empirical evidence is statistically weak. No confidence intervals, repeated-seed variation, or significance tests are provided. AmbiSem-3D has only 21 manually designed cases; the 100-case extension compares only against SAM3D and reports two CLIP metrics. The very large user-study preference gap is difficult to assess because the manuscript omits interface, randomization, rating protocol, per-case aggregation, uncertainty, participant screening, and hypothesis tests.

The proposed multi-prior “consensus” mechanism lacks justification: simply concatenating tokens before softmax does not guarantee that shared semantic attributes receive greater aggregate attention. Equation 8 additionally smooths flattened query and key indices, including across concatenated-prior boundaries, although these sequence coordinates are not shown to define a meaningful spatial frequency domain. Relevant ablations comparing concatenation with independent-prior averaging or controlling boundary smoothing are absent.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a method built from many inference interventions. The paper does not provide code or a release commitment for the benchmarks, and omits such details as solver step count, exact attention layers/heads modified, token ordering and boundary handling, prior-generation seeds, sampling seeds, and complete benchmark annotations. Licensing and redistribution conditions for derived datasets and generated/commercial-model outputs are also not discussed.

Ethics treatment is too generic. The impact statement acknowledges misuse and bias, but the study reports 32 human participants without discussing consent, compensation, recruitment, privacy, or institutional review/exemption. This is not necessarily a harmful study, but appropriate human-subject reporting is missing.

Presentation contains multiple inconsistencies that impede verification: theorem/proposition numbering differs between the main text and appendix, symbols and conditioning arguments change within proofs, alpha_max is introduced without a valid derivation, and the paper characterizes Wasserstein distance as directly ensuring geometrically plausible shapes although the bound operates over unspecified latent/output distributions.

Overall, the task and pipeline are promising, but the paper’s strongest theoretical claims are materially unsupported and its metrics do not validate the defining requirement of strict visible-evidence preservation. These are central rather than cosmetic issues, so the current version does not meet the technical-evidence threshold for acceptance.

strengths: Soundness: The dual-branch design is technically plausible and well motivated: observation-conditioned velocities preserve visible evidence, semantic-prior velocities steer ambiguous regions, and visibility-aware blending limits unwanted changes to observed surfaces.

Empirical evidence: RelaxFlow improves both tested backbones on ExtremeOcc-3D. With SAM3D, CLIP-text rises from 24.08 to 27.26, FID falls from 50.73 to 39.44, and Point-FID falls from 100.38 to 81.11, while CLIP-image and LPIPS also improve. Component ablations support the contributions of relaxation and visibility masking.

Significance: Text-controlled amodal 3D completion is a useful formulation for genuinely underdetermined observations. The training-free nature and demonstrations on both SAM3D and TRELLIS make the approach practically relevant.

Originality: The method offers a novel synthesis of multiple visual priors, relaxed semantic guidance, time-dependent velocity fusion, and spatial visibility control. ExtremeOcc-3D and AmbiSem-3D are useful diagnostic benchmarks for failure modes poorly covered by standard image-to-3D evaluation.

Presentation: The motivation, pipeline, qualitative comparisons, implementation defaults, computational overhead, and failure cases are presented clearly. The visual examples compellingly demonstrate different prompt-conditioned completions of the same observation.

Limitations and ethics: The paper honestly identifies failure under mutually incompatible conditions and reports the substantial 1.82–2.46× runtime overhead. Its impact statement recognizes misuse and bias risks without treating these admissions as evidence against the contribution.
weaknesses: Soundness—theory: The claimed equivalence between attention-logit smoothing and low-pass filtering of the generative vector field is not established. Appendix A.4 assumes only Lipschitz dependence on logits, which bounds the magnitude of the velocity change but does not show that high-frequency velocity components or semantic error are suppressed.

Soundness—theory: Proposition A.4 informally replaces v_sem−G*v_theta with G*(v_sem−v_theta), omitting the signal-distortion term (I−G)*v_sem. Approximate band limitation and qualitative high-frequency dominance are insufficient for the stated strict error reduction without quantitative bounds. Several stability derivations also use inconsistent conditioning notation and appear to treat the time-varying alpha as constant outside integrals. Consequently, the Wasserstein results are conditional intuition rather than a meaningful guarantee for the implemented method; a tighter upper bound would not itself prove lower realized W2 distance.

Evaluation scale: The principal ambiguity benchmark contains only 21 manually designed cases. The 100-case extension compares only against SAM3D and reports two CLIP metrics, so it does not provide the full baseline, user-study, or 3D-quality evidence needed to establish broad generalization.

Evaluation rigor: The paper reports no confidence intervals, repeated-seed variation, or significance tests. This is especially important for the modest automatic-metric differences on AmbiSem-3D and for FID/Point-FID estimated from relatively small, correlated multi-view samples.

User study: Although 32 volunteers evaluate 21 cases, essential protocol details are missing, including the number and construction of trials, randomization and blinding, rating versus forced-choice procedure, participant screening, aggregation, uncertainty, and consent or compensation. The percentages in Table 2 are therefore difficult to interpret or audit.

Metric validity and claims: Minimum LPIPS over ten rendered views can reward viewpoint search rather than strict preservation at the known observation camera. CLIP and set-level FID-style measures do not directly verify geometric consistency or pixel-level preservation. Thus, the strong claim that observation fidelity is preserved “strictly” is not fully supported by the reported metrics.

Reproducibility: Useful hyperparameters and hardware costs are given, but the manuscript does not state that code, benchmark annotations, or evaluation scripts will be released. It also omits important details such as checkpoints, solver step counts, modified attention layers, random seeds, prior-generation seeds, baseline tuning, and complete rendering/user-study protocols.

Originality is primarily compositional: dual-branch guidance, attention smoothing, multi-prior conditioning, and visibility masks each have close precedents. The contribution is still useful, but the paper overstates the theoretical novelty and strength of its guarantees. A more precise positioning and removal or repair of the proof-level claims would materially strengthen the work.
